_note: Maths reasoning cases: a situation, the information given, a question and candidate answers, in two versions. Solve, where the numbers settle it and every wrong answer is ruled out by a line of the problem. Debate, where a line has been changed and more than one answer holds up if the student says what it assumes. Written by hand in scripts/math-cases/g<N>.json and folded together by scripts/merge-math-cases.mjs; do not edit this file by hand. scripts/check-math-cases.mjs re-derives every solve answer and holds the structure to its rules.

cases.title: The Case of the Empty Chair
given: 8 children came to story time.
There are 6 chairs in the circle.
Every child wants a chair.
Nobody brings in more chairs.
cases.question: How many children have no chair?

rules_out.why: 6 is how many chairs there are, not how many children are left standing.
8 is every child who came, and 6 of them do get a chair.
Only 8 children came, so 14 of them cannot be left out.

cases.explain: Match one child to one chair. Six pairs up, and the children left over are the answer: 8 take away 6 is 2.

given: 8 children came to story time.
There are 6 chairs in the circle.
2 children chose to sit on the rug.
1 chair is broken and wobbles.
debate.question: How many children have no chair? Say which words you used.

arguments.why: 8 children and 6 chairs leaves 2 children standing.
A broken chair is not a chair to sit on, so only 5 of them work: 8 take away 5 is 3.
2 children chose the rug, so the other 6 each had one of the 6 chairs and nobody was left out.

debate.note: All three can be argued. What settles it is what counts as a chair and what counts as wanting one, so make the child say which words they used.

cases.title: The Case of the Book Box
given: On Monday the box held 15 books.
On Tuesday the class took out 6 books.
On Wednesday 4 books were put back.
Nobody else opened the box.
cases.question: How many books are in the box now?

rules_out.why: 9 is where the box was on Tuesday night. On Wednesday 4 books came back.
Adding all three numbers counts the books that left as if they had arrived.
The 4 books on Wednesday went in, so they are added, not taken away.

cases.explain: Walk the days in order: 15, take 6 away to get 9, put 4 back to get 13. The order of the days tells you which way each number goes.

given: On Monday the box held 15 books.
On Tuesday the class took out 6 books.
On Wednesday 4 books were put back.
Two of the books put back came from the library, not from this box.
debate.question: How many of the box's own books are in the box now?

arguments.why: Count what is in the box, whoever owns it. Four books went in: 15 take away 6, add 4, is 13.
The question asks for the box's own books. Only 2 of the 4 belong here: 15 take away 6, add 2, is 11.
None of the 6 that left has come back. The books put back are different books, so the box's own count is 15 take away 6, which is 9.

debate.note: The argument is about what the question is counting: books in the box, or books that belong to the box. Both readings are honest, and saying which one you chose is the mathematics.

cases.title: The Case of the Change That Felt Wrong
given: Sam pays with 3 quarters, 2 dimes and 4 pennies.
The book costs 84 cents.
A quarter is 25 cents, a dime is 10 cents, a penny is 1 cent.
Sam gets his change in pennies.
cases.question: How many pennies of change should Sam get?

rules_out.why: 99 cents is what Sam handed over. The price of the book still has to come off it.
9 counts the coins. The line of values says what each coin is worth, and a quarter is not worth the same as a penny.
84 cents is the price of the book, not the change from it.

cases.explain: Turn the coins into cents first: 75 and 20 and 4 make 99. The change is what is left once the price comes off: 99 take away 84 is 15 pennies.

given: Sam pays with 3 quarters, 2 dimes and 4 pennies.
The sign under the book says 84 cents.
The till rings it up at 79 cents.
A quarter is 25 cents, a dime is 10 cents, a penny is 1 cent.
debate.question: How much change should Sam get? Say which number you trusted, and why.

arguments.why: The sign is the price the shop put on the book: 99 take away 84 is 15.
The till is the price the shop is charging now: 99 take away 79 is 20.

debate.note: Both children can do the subtraction. What they are arguing about is which number is the price, and that is an argument shops have with customers every day.

cases.title: The Case of the Short Tray
given: The class baked 6 trays of cookies.
A full tray holds 4 cookies.
One tray came out of the oven with 1 cookie missing.
Nobody ate any.
cases.question: How many cookies did the class bake?

rules_out.why: 24 is six full trays, and one of the trays was not full.
Adding the trays to the cookies-per-tray counts neither of them. Four cookies on each of six trays is a multiplication.
A missing cookie comes off the total, not on.

cases.explain: Equal groups first: six fours is 24. Then the one line that breaks the pattern: a cookie is missing, so 23.

given: The class baked 6 trays of cookies.
A full tray holds 4 cookies.
Two trays came out with gaps in them.
Nobody counted the gaps.
debate.question: How many cookies did the class bake? Give a number you can defend.

arguments.why: Six trays of four is 24. The gaps were never counted, so there is no number to take away.
A gap is at least one cookie and two trays have gaps, so 24 take away 2 is the most we can still claim.
If a tray with gaps cannot be counted at all, only the four full trays count: four fours is 16.

debate.note: This is the difference between a number and an estimate. 24 is the most there can be, 16 the least, and the honest answer says which of the two it is.

cases.title: The Case of the Shared Ribbon
given: The roll held 3 metres of ribbon.
Mia used 3/4 of a metre.
Jo used 1 1/2 metres.
Nothing else was cut from the roll.
cases.question: How many metres of ribbon are left?

rules_out.why: Only Mia's piece has come off. Jo cut some too.
Only Jo's piece has come off. Mia cut 3/4 of a metre as well.
1 1/2 is one and a half, not one. The extra half metre is still missing from the subtraction.

cases.explain: Put everything over the same denominator: 3 metres is 12/4, Mia took 3/4, Jo took 6/4. 12/4 minus 3/4 minus 6/4 leaves 3/4 of a metre.

given: The roll held 3 metres of ribbon.
Mia used 3/4 of a metre.
Jo used about one and a half metres.
The scraps under the table come to 1/4 of a metre altogether.
debate.question: How much usable ribbon is left? Defend your number.

arguments.why: Take off what was used: 3 minus 3/4 minus 1 1/2 leaves 3/4 of a metre on the roll.
Scraps are not usable length, so they come off too: 3/4 minus 1/4 is 1/2 a metre.
'About one and a half' could be a little under, and a 1/4 metre of scraps still cuts short pieces, so close to a metre is defensible.

debate.note: The word 'about' is doing the work here. Ask which numbers in the problem are exact and which one is a measurement, because only one of them can be argued with.

cases.title: The Case of the Receipt That Rang Twice
given: The receipt lists milk at 3.49, bread at 2.75 and eggs at 4.20.
The total printed at the bottom is 13.19.
The shop charges no tax on food.
Exactly one item was scanned twice.
cases.question: Which item was scanned twice? Give its price in dollars.

rules_out.why: Milk twice would make the total 13.93, and the receipt says 13.19.
Eggs twice would make the total 14.64, and the receipt says 13.19.
10.44 is what the three items come to once each, which is what the receipt should have printed, not what it did print.

cases.explain: Add the three listed prices: 10.44. The receipt took 13.19, so the overcharge is 13.19 minus 10.44, which is 2.75 — and 2.75 is the bread.

given: The receipt lists milk at 3.49, bread at 2.75 and eggs at 4.20.
The total printed is 13.19.
There are two loaves of bread in the bag.
The shop adds a 2.75 crate charge to delivery orders, and this was a delivery.
debate.question: How much, if anything, should the shop refund? Defend the number.

arguments.why: The three listed prices come to 10.44. The receipt took 2.75 more than it lists, and a charge that is not printed should come back.
The 2.75 is the crate charge on a delivery. The total is right; the receipt simply does not print that line.
If the 2.75 is the crate, then the second loaf in the bag has not been paid for at all, and the customer owes 2.75 rather than being owed it.

debate.note: Every one of these is arithmetic a fifth grader can do. What they are arguing about is which story the numbers are evidence for, which is the whole of modelling.

cases.title: The Case of the Better Buy
given: The small box holds 12 ounces and costs 3.60.
The large box holds 20 ounces and costs 5.40.
Both boxes hold exactly the same cereal.
Neither box is on special offer.
cases.question: What is the price per ounce of the better buy, in dollars?

rules_out.why: 0.30 is the small box's rate, and it is the higher of the two.
0.225 is the price of the extra ounces only — 1.80 more for 8 more ounces — not the price per ounce of a box.
1.80 is how much more the large box costs altogether. It is a difference, not a rate.

cases.explain: A rate is price divided by amount. 3.60 over 12 ounces is 0.30 an ounce; 5.40 over 20 ounces is 0.27 an ounce. Lower is better, so the large box.

given: The small box holds 12 ounces and costs 3.60.
The large box holds 20 ounces and costs 5.40.
This family eats a box a week and throws out about 4 ounces of a large box gone stale.
There is shelf room for one box at a time.
debate.question: Which box is the better buy for this family? Give the rate you are using.

options.label: 0.3375 an ounce eaten, the large box

arguments.why: Per ounce bought, the large box is cheaper: 5.40 over 20 is 0.27.
Per ounce eaten, the large box is 5.40 over 16, which is 0.3375 — worse than the small box.
If the waste is real, the small box at 0.30 an ounce with nothing thrown away is the better buy.

debate.note: Nobody is disputing the arithmetic; they are disputing the denominator. Ask each student what they divided by, and why that is the right amount to divide by.

cases.title: The Case of the Two Discounts
given: The jacket is marked 80 dollars.
The sign says 25 percent off.
A coupon takes 10 dollars off at the till.
The store takes the percentage off first, then the coupon.
cases.question: What does the jacket cost at the till, in dollars?

rules_out.why: 52.50 is the coupon taken off first and the 25 percent off what was left. The store does it the other way round.
60 is the sale price before the coupon is handed over.
45 treats 25 percent as 25 dollars. A percentage is of something, and 25 percent of 80 is 20.

cases.explain: 25 percent of 80 is 20, so the sale price is 60. The coupon is a flat 10 off that, giving 50. Order matters here: coupon first would have given 52.50.

given: The jacket is marked 80 dollars.
The sign says 25 percent off.
A coupon takes 10 dollars off.
The coupon is printed 'cannot be combined with other offers'.
debate.question: What should the customer pay? Defend it.

arguments.why: Nothing in the arithmetic stops both: 60, then 10 off, is 50. 'Other offers' may well mean other coupons rather than the store's own sale.
The coupon cannot be combined, so the customer takes whichever is better. 25 percent off is 60, and that beats the coupon.
If the customer hands over the coupon, that is the offer they chose: 80 minus 10 is 70. It is the worse deal, but it is what the rule allows.

debate.note: All three are computed correctly. The disagreement is over what one sentence in the problem means, which is exactly the argument a shop has with a customer.

cases.title: The Case of the Identical Bills
given: Plan A charges 20 dollars a month plus 0.10 a minute.
Plan B charges 35 dollars a month and nothing per minute.
Both plans bill whole months.
Last month the two bills came to exactly the same amount.
cases.question: How many minutes were used last month?

rules_out.why: 15 is the gap between the two monthly charges in dollars. It becomes minutes only after it is divided by the per-minute rate.
350 is what 35 dollars buys at 10 cents a minute, which ignores Plan A's own 20-dollar monthly charge.
550 comes from adding the two monthly charges. The bills were equal, not combined.

cases.explain: Set the two costs equal: 20 + 0.10m = 35. The fixed charges differ by 15 dollars, and at 10 cents a minute that gap takes 150 minutes to close. Below 150 minutes Plan A is cheaper; above it, Plan B.

given: Plan A charges 20 dollars a month plus 0.10 a minute.
Plan B charges 35 dollars a month and nothing per minute.
The family used 150 minutes last month and 400 the month before.
Next month is the school holidays.
debate.question: Which plan should the family choose? Name the number of minutes your answer rests on.

arguments.why: At 150 minutes the plans cost the same, and the most recent month is the best evidence of the next one. At or below 150, Plan A wins.
The two months average 275 minutes, which is well past the 150-minute crossing point, so Plan B.
The holidays are the heavier month, and 400 minutes costs 60 dollars on Plan A against 35 on Plan B. Plan for the heavy month.

debate.note: The algebra is settled: the plans cross at 150 minutes. What is not settled is which month predicts next month, and that is a modelling choice rather than an arithmetic mistake.

cases.title: The Case of the Spreading Rumour
given: On day 1, 4 students had heard the rumour.
On day 2, 8 students had heard it.
On day 3, 16 students had heard it.
The school has 512 students, and the question is day 6.
cases.question: If the pattern holds, how many students have heard it on day 6?

rules_out.why: 24 comes from adding 4 a day. That would put day 3 at 12, and day 3 is 16.
64 is day 5. Day 1 already has 4 students, so the doubling happens five times to reach day 6, not four.
512 is the whole school. The pattern does not reach it until day 8.

cases.explain: Each day the number doubles: 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Multiplying by the same factor each step is what makes this exponential rather than linear — a linear pattern adds the same amount each step instead.

given: On day 1, 4 students had heard the rumour.
On day 2, 8 students had heard it.
On day 3, 16 students had heard it.
The school has 512 students, and 180 of them are away on a trip all week.
debate.question: How many will have heard it on day 6? Say what your model assumes.

arguments.why: Doubling from 4 gives 128 on day 6, and nothing in the three days of data breaks the pattern.
With 180 students away, each student who knows has fewer people left to tell, so growth slows before day 6 and something under 128 is the honest figure.
Doubling cannot pass the 332 students actually in the building. The curve has to flatten, and 332 is the ceiling it flattens against.

debate.note: Three days of data fit a doubling and fit the start of an S-curve equally well. Exponential models are always true at the beginning and never true at the end, and naming where yours stops being true is the skill.

cases.title: The Case of the Paint That Came Out Exact
given: The wall is 24 feet long and 9 feet high.
One tin covers 130 square feet.
The wall needs two coats.
A door 3 feet by 7 feet is not painted.
cases.question: How many tins does the job need?

rules_out.why: One coat of 195 square feet is a tin and a half. The wall takes two coats.
4 tins comes from painting the whole 216 square feet twice. The door's 21 square feet are not painted at all, let alone twice.
The two coats are already inside the 390 square feet. Doubling the tins as well pays for four coats.

cases.explain: Paintable area is the wall minus the door: 216 minus 21 is 195 square feet. Two coats make 390. At 130 square feet a tin, that is exactly 3 tins.

given: The wall is 24 feet long and 9 feet high.
One tin covers 130 square feet.
The wall needs two coats, and the first coat on bare plaster soaks in.
A door 3 feet by 7 feet is not painted, and the shop sells tins singly with no returns.
debate.question: How many tins should they buy? Defend the number.

arguments.why: 390 square feet at 130 a tin is exactly 3 tins, with nothing bought that is not used.
A first coat that soaks into bare plaster covers less than 130 square feet, so exactly 3 tins will run out somewhere near the end. Buy the spare.
Bare plaster often wants a third coat in patches and the shop takes no returns, so buy for the job you may find rather than the job on paper.

debate.note: The geometry gives exactly 3, which is the most dangerous answer in the room: a model that comes out exact has left itself no room for the thing the model ignored. Ask what each extra tin is buying.

cases.title: The Case of the Line That Went Too Far
given: A bean plant was measured each week: 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14 centimetres.
Those are weeks 1 to 5, and the prediction wanted is for week 20.
The line of best fit through the five points is h = 3w - 1.
Beans of this kind stop growing at about 60 centimetres.
cases.question: What height does the line predict at week 20, in centimetres?

rules_out.why: 60 is where this kind of bean stops growing. It is a fact about the plant, not what the line says.
57 takes the 1 off the week rather than off the height: that is 3 times 19, not 3 times 20 minus 1.
14 cm is the last measurement taken, at week 5.

cases.explain: Substituting w = 20 into h = 3w - 1 gives 59. That is what the line says. Whether the plant says it is a different question, and it is the one worth asking.

given: A bean plant measured 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14 centimetres in weeks 1 to 5.
The line of best fit is h = 3w - 1, and it passes within 0.2 cm of every point.
Beans of this kind stop growing at about 60 centimetres.
Week 20 falls in late August, after the plant has flowered.
debate.question: What should they predict for week 20? Say how far you trust it.

arguments.why: The line fits five points to within 0.2 cm. Inside the data it is excellent, and what it gives at week 20 is 59.
Growth flattens as a plant nears its limit, so the honest prediction is the limit itself, about 60.
A plant that has flowered puts its energy into seed rather than height. Growth stops before the ceiling, so a figure well short of 59 is defensible.

debate.note: A fit of 0.2 cm over five weeks says nothing whatever about week 20. Ask every student to name the range of weeks they would trust their line across, and to say why the range ends where it does.

cases.title: The Case of the Test That Is Almost Always Right
given: 1 student in 100 at the school has the condition.
The test comes back positive for every student who has it.
The test also comes back positive for 5 percent of the students who do not have it.
All 2000 students are tested.
cases.question: How many students test positive altogether?

rules_out.why: 20 students have the condition, and they are not the only ones the test calls positive.
100 is 5 percent of the whole school, which treats the 20 who have the condition as though they were healthy.
120 adds 5 percent of all 2000 to the 20 real cases, counting those 20 twice.

cases.explain: 20 students have it, and every one of them tests positive. Of the 1980 who do not, 5 percent — 99 students — test positive too. That is 119 positives, of which 20 are real: fewer than one positive in five means anything.

given: 1 student in 100 has the condition, and all 2000 students are tested.
The test is positive for everyone who has it, and for 5 percent of those who do not.
One particular student has tested positive.
That student also has two of the three symptoms the condition causes.
debate.question: How likely is it that this student has the condition? Give a number you can defend.

arguments.why: Of 2000 students, 119 test positive and 20 of those have it. On the test alone the chance is 20 in 119, about 17 percent.
The symptoms are evidence the base rate never saw. Conditioning on the test and the symptoms together puts the figure well above 17 percent.
If two of three symptoms are rare in healthy students, the chance climbs steeply — though how steeply needs a number this problem does not give.

debate.note: Only the first number comes from the arithmetic on the page, and it is the one that surprises people. The second and third are right in principle and cannot be pinned down from what is given, which is itself worth saying out loud: the answer is low, and more evidence would raise it, and we are not told by how much.
